reviews.text: 总结：好玩，爱玩，没玩过；但是现在买有点太早了 免费试玩的时候看到B站up蜥蜴君玩所以试了一下，很新鲜很有趣。我倒是也没玩过很多类似的但是因为自己就是程序员所以觉得很有梗就首发直接入了。不明就里底吐槽了人物和地图过少的问题但是其实是我自己太菜没解锁，向开发者们说声抱歉！ 下班回家还是愿意开一把的，一边玩一边希望自己写的程序也能和游戏里一样健壮，别动不动就崩溃了... 但是就现在而言确实游戏没有一个完整的样子，局外成长没有（如果你觉得这才是纯血rouge那就是你对），感觉代码块的种类也不是很丰富，记得我第一天玩的时候就磁铁可以吸取经验宝石的，后来就没再见过。 我反正经常会打开看的，期待有一天能好评！加油！

My only minor critique, which might be more of a personal issue, is that the characters seem a bit AI generated. If they had a full body and weren't just a portrait I think that would solve the issue but again this might just be something I personally think that doesn't bother others. I recommend this game if you like hacking and garlic.

考虑到折后20元左右的价格，是推荐体验的，但不建议原价购买。 游戏本身也只能体验，没什么深入游玩的必要与潜力。 游戏性质的话，远没有看起来这么复杂，甚至简单而简陋，所有流派都是简单的寻找乘区。 不能说很无聊，对我来说比吸血鬼幸存者有趣，至少有一点点思考，垃圾时间没那么垃圾。 至少对游戏理解不完全的情况下，对局内前中期的构筑感是强于吸血鬼等的，也不依赖外部信息，是很不错的一段体验。 但不“无聊”，并没有多有趣，重复的那些节点，一样的思考与思路，很快就下头了。 20元，前2小时摸索，中6小时上头，后4小时熟练轻松，然后慢慢变无聊和刷子，解锁新角色的时候小小兴奋一下，但看着重复的节点和思路又开始犯恶心。 不算不可接受，但显然不怎么好。 具体来说。 地图和敌人基本没有差异度，甚至外形都没什么差异，也没有BOSS。 局外成长影响非常大，差一半伤害和经济的情况下，游戏直接前几次难5几乎不可能打赢。 角色的差异只有一个初始节点（局内可以获得），一点被动属性（血量或速度，局内可以获得），没了。 BUG和未描述内容很多，放在别的游戏不是大问题，但这么逻辑的游戏数据缺失这么多，就很不舒服了。 比如感染系的遍历需要额外遍历或选中才能生效（常规是子弹命中的敌人自动判定为下一个节点的释放点），直接导致整个流派都很弱。 比如很多技能的范围，发射距离和爆炸范围，很多概率类的东西，都没有展示。 游戏时长很长，是因为退出游戏没法彻底关闭，除非关闭steam…… 局外成长靠游戏内占领据点，但与此同时高难又会需要一些走位（尤其前中期），局外收益和游戏胜利互相矛盾，很拧巴。 不同初始节点的组合，强度差距不小。想要解锁角色的不同初始节点，要累计难5、难10，要么打两个地图的难2难3，要么拿弱势的初始组合，打一个地图难5，也很拧巴。

I’m genuinely impressed. As someone with little programming experience, I was worried the visual node system would be intimidating—but it’s incredibly intuitive. The drag-and-drop interface lets you experiment freely, and I’ve actually picked up some useful logic concepts that translate well to Python and GDScript. No prior coding knowledge is needed; just play around and see what happens. What keeps it fresh after dozens of runs is the sheer variety. With 190+ nodes, 13 characters, modifiers, and enhancements, I keep discovering new synergies. It never feels stagnant. The roguelite loop is also refreshingly non-punishing—failures don’t feel like dead ends. A quick trip to the Dark Market to upgrade or swapping characters keeps the momentum going. The “no RNG” claim isn’t 100% accurate (you do get random node drops and enemy loot), but it’s fair. Getting lucky early can turn a run into a power fantasy, but skill and smart node chaining still matter. The difficulty curve is challenging but fair—even for a non-pro gamer like me. Roadblocks exist, but they’re surmountable with persistence. Each character feels distinct, boosting different node families, which encourages finding a playstyle that matches your thinking (or blasting) preferences. And for Linux users: it runs flawlessly on Arch. No tweaks needed.

An update just dropped which claimed to add "controller support". This is a lie. The update allows controllers to use the same (clunky, bug-riddled) mouse and keyboard interface using the analog stick and A button. That is not "support". There are no menus or grids, you just have to try to drag and drop, and hope the random tooltips don't get in the way of where you want to place things. Even the Level Up screen, which has 3 options and should have been low hanging fruit, is selected from using the cursor. The patch notes state things that are flat-out incorrect, such as "Tooltips are no longer displayed when dragging or connecting a node". They also specifically mention an improved experience for Steam Deck players, but the lag on that system renders it effectively unplayable. It's a shame because before this update, if I had been intending to play while sitting at a desktop computer, it probably would have been a thumbs up, but deceptively trying to sneak a slice of the Steam Deck pie without actually working for it is something that potential buyers now have to be warned against.

I wanted to like this game and I did for a little bit. Combining different nodes to make powerful weapons is fun. The problem is that this is pretty much the limit of the fun in the game. The level design is basically nonexistent. Every level is nearly identical with just some minor visual changes. Likewise, the enemies are all very samey. Each run consists of a series of layers (it's always been 7 so far, not sure if that changes at some point). You get a set amount of time on each layer. Each layer consists of fighting off enemies while you wander around to specific points to download data which maps to a meta-currency you use for permanent progression. When the time runs out, you go to the exit. Rinse and repeat until you finish layer 7 and you're done. The biggest problem with this is that there is almost no variety. There are a small number of different weapon types (a single shot, a damage area, a spinning projectile, and a mine) so your build is nearly identical each run. There's nothing like Vampire Survivor where you have a wide variety of different weapons and playstyles. The level up rewards are all simple stat boosts (increased range, damage, etc.). They don't meaningfully change the feel of a run. There's also nothing like Vampire Survivors' evolution system. There's nothing you're ever trying to achieve with your build. There's no thoughts of, "Oh, if I can find X item then I can do Y." Again, very samey. Speaking of Vampire Survivors, part of what made that game great was the relics and exploration. The levels are large and you can learn them and use them to your advantage. They also contain secrets, like coffins that unlock other characters or relics that unlock features. There's nothing like that in this game. There is nothing to drive me to explore or play the next level other than the progression treadmill. And that progression treadmill is sloooooooow. I'm 4 hours in and I've only managed to get a single character to their first upgrade and I've barely scratched the surface of the permanent upgrades. It's going to easily take 100+ hours to grind through everything. I'll say this. I paid $4 for the game and I got $4 worth of value out of it. If the game looks at all interesting to you and you can find it for cheap, go for it. Just know what to expect.

[h2]A Wasted Great Idea[/h2] Net.Attack stumbled badly with its Roguelike elements, and that’s a flaw that overshadows much of the experience. The game’s modular effects and programming logic, where you splice together inputs, outputs, and modifiers to enhance your damage or survivability, are genuinely interesting. Like... Seriously? Well done. The satisfaction comes from cleverly combining values and effects, making each run potentially more unique than the last in how you approach the RNG challenge of mixing around these modules. Unfortunately, the Roguelike foundation lets everything down. Each run is a slog through the same uninspired motherboard stage, fighting the same repetitive enemies, and waiting for them to wander close enough for you to wipe them out with your optimized build. There’s no real sense of discovery, escalation, or tension, just a satisfyingly slow crawl. Even the promise of unlocking new characters or game modes in the future doesn’t do much to relieve the monotony. Ultimately, Net.Attack’s core gameplay loop is simply not fun or rewarding enough to make you want to keep playing. But that logic behing the programming again, top tier stuff. It's just unfortunate that the rest of the game couldn't live up to that same level of creativity.
